site.name: Sam Kemmis
site.tagline: A year of things I built with AI coding agents.
site.intro: Games, prediction-market tools, and a few analyses. Every one of these was vibe coded: I described what I wanted, an agent wrote the code, and we argued about it until it worked. The ones that didn't work aren't here, but there were plenty.

groups.label: Play
groups.blurb: Games you can open in a browser right now.

groups.blurb: Prediction-market tools, mostly built around Kalshi.

groups.label: Read
groups.blurb: Data stories and the newsletter that runs on them.

projects.name: Fantasy Reality
projects.one: A fantasy league for prediction markets.
projects.description: Seasons, leagues, parlays, and a shared wallet, all scored against real Kalshi and Polymarket prices. AI players bet alongside humans, a weekly digest goes out by email, and a Discord bot nags the league when a week is empty. It started as "VibeBet" on Replit in December 2025 and became the project every other one on this page grew out of.
projects.notes: The rule that caused the most bugs: the season is the economy, a league is only a grouping of people.

projects.name: DegenBench
projects.one: Frontier AI models paper-bet on real markets, every day.
stack: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI SDKs
projects.description: Each model gets the same slate of Kalshi markets and its own web search. Round one is an independent forecast with a public argument. Round two, every model reads the others' anonymized arguments and submits a final probability and an optional bet from a virtual bankroll. Scored on Brier score against a market-implied baseline, and on profit, because that's the degen metric.
projects.notes: All paper trading. No real money, no orders placed.

projects.name: Kalshi Mention Tracker
projects.one: Which words will he say? A phrase-market database.
projects.description: Kalshi runs markets on whether a speaker will say a given phrase. This tracks every one of them: phrase search, per-phrase timelines, and an event log with settled outcomes, so you can see how often "tariff" actually gets said before you bet on it. The standalone version was built in Lovable in an afternoon; it was later folded into Fantasy Reality, where it feeds the research behind the newsletter.

projects.name: Fantasy Reality Newsletter
projects.one: A Substack about prediction markets, plus the chart-maker behind it.
projects.description: The newsletter is the human part. The tool is a three-step wizard: paste a Kalshi event URL, frame the window and the y-axis, drop annotations on the chart, and export a PNG in the house style. There's an editorial preset and a louder meme preset with pixel callout boxes. Every chart saves a story file so the GitHub Action can re-render it later.
projects.notes: A companion branch holds a video pipeline for a Kalshi market video series, one episode in.

projects.name: Emberfall
projects.one: A real-time online table for a cooperative Middle-earth board game.
projects.description: Two to five players, each running two characters, escorting Frodo to Mount Doom from different living rooms. The host shares a four-letter room code. The engine only offers legal moves, every location, stat, die face and card is hover-documented, and dice rolls pause in a resolution panel so anyone present can spend a resource before the roll is locked in. Reloading rejoins your seat with the full log restored.
projects.notes: Rules paraphrased from the publisher's rulebook, no art or card text copied. Not affiliated with anyone. Buy the real game.

projects.name: Music for Parking
projects.one: A day of Los Angeles parking tickets, replayed on the hour, as music.
projects.description: Real parking citations from the city's open-data feed, replayed across a map of LA on the hour. Each ticket is a note, and the neighborhoods keep their own rhythm, so the city becomes a slow generative score. It's the shippable slice of a much bigger idea, a territory game on a real hex map fed by LA's own data, with a lore bible that runs from Horace Bell to Manly P. Hall to Didion. The game part is still in the repo, waiting.

projects.name: Sex House Island
projects.one: The first fully autonomous season of reality TV, and the engine to play it.
projects.description: A promotional site for a reality show that doesn't exist: eight cast members, a remote island, prediction markets on who gets eliminated, and an investor page. Underneath it is the real experiment, a LucasArts-style point-and-click engine in about six hundred lines of TypeScript and Canvas. Nine verbs, a sentence line, hotspots, inventory combinations, a parrot with a dialogue tree, and a three-step puzzle. The walk cycle is drawn in code so the engine could be felt before any sprite existed.
projects.notes: Answer to the question it was built to ask: the engine is the easy part. The art is the hard part.

projects.name: Gizzard Hours
projects.one: How much King Gizzard, actually, from a YouTube history export.
projects.description: Google Takeout ships your watch history as one 67 MB HTML file with no newlines. This streams it in chunks, fingerprints the band by channel ID, matches every play against a cached MusicBrainz discography of 265 releases, and reconstructs listening time by month, by album, and by how heavy the album is. Then it does the same for the Disney catalogue, for comparison. It fed an essay on the newsletter.

projects.name: Pre-Speech Odds vs. Reality
projects.one: Fifteen months of Trump mention markets: is anyone an insider?
projects.description: Every price, trade and transcript for 159 speeches. Speech starts are recovered from the moment a phrase's contract pins to 99 cents. The crowd overpays for coin-flips, ignores each phrase's own track record, and keeps paying for words he has stopped saying. Insiders, though, didn't show up: 92 suspicious contracts hit exactly as often as their prices claimed.

projects.name: Chameleon Resume
projects.one: Paste a job posting and it tells you whether I'm a fit.
projects.description: A resume that meets the reader halfway. Paste a job posting URL and it reads the role, scores the fit against my background, and reorders what it shows you to match. The rest of the page is a conventional resume for people who'd rather just read one.
projects.notes: Built in Lovable, which is also why it's the only thing here I can't show you the code for.
